paragraphes: Your school cafeteria does not make everything itself. The bread comes from a bakery. The yogurts come from a factory.
One day, a batch of yogurts is bad at the factory. Nobody in the cafeteria did anything wrong. Still, many students feel sick.
Companies have the same problem with their machines, programs, and services. This is called supply chain risk.

decouverte.comme: A bike chain is strong only if every link is strong. One rusty link, and the chain breaks.
decouverte.enVrai: The supply chain is all the suppliers that a company needs. They give it hardware (machines you can touch), software (programs), or services. A supplier is also called a vendor. Each vendor is one link. The picture stops here: you can see a rusty link, but you often cannot see a risk at a vendor.

decouverte.question: Your school needs a new yogurt supplier. What should it do before it signs?
options: Check how the supplier works
Pick the cheapest supplier
Choose the best-known name
decouverte.explanation: The school trusts the supplier with its students' health. So it must check first. A low price and a famous name look good, but they do not prove quality.

decouverte.texte: A company wants to keep its data with a cloud provider. A cloud provider (CSP) is a company that rents out computers over the internet. The provider keeps the data in another country. The law of your country may not allow that. No hacker is needed here. A rule of law or contract is not followed. This is called a compliance risk.

cards.question: Official definition: “supply chain”
cards.answer: Securing your organization's assets requires that you evaluate the security risk of your entire supply chain and that you apply appropriate controls to manage that risk.
cards.explanation: In simple words: find out how risky all your suppliers are. Then use the right controls. An asset is anything of value, like data or machines.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Apply Supply Chain Risk Management Concepts”.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “supply chain”?
options: Securing your organization's assets requires that you evaluate the security risk of your entire supply chain and that you apply appropriate controls to manage that risk.
Securing your organization's assets requires that you evaluate the security risk of your own systems and that you apply appropriate controls to manage that risk.
Securing your organization's assets requires that you evaluate the security risk of your entire supply chain and that you remove all risk from it.
Securing your organization's assets requires that you evaluate the security risk of your largest suppliers and that you apply appropriate controls to manage that risk.
options_why: It looks only at your own systems. The real sentence says the entire supply chain.
Nobody can remove all risk. The real sentence says to manage the risk with appropriate controls.
Small suppliers can be a weak link too. The real sentence says the entire supply chain.
cards.answer: Securing your organization's assets requires that you evaluate the security risk of your entire supply chain and that you apply appropriate controls to manage that risk.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: evaluate the security risk, entire supply chain, appropriate controls.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “supply chain” from memory.
cards.answer: Securing your organization's assets requires that you evaluate the security risk of your entire supply chain and that you apply appropriate controls to manage that risk.
cards.explanation: Two moves: evaluate the risk of the whole chain, then apply the right controls.

cards.question: A cloud provider keeps your data in a country where the law does not allow it. What kind of risk is this?
options: A risk of broken hardware
A risk of a typing mistake by a worker
A risk that only hackers can cause
A compliance risk
options_why: No machine is broken here. The problem is a rule that is not followed.
Nobody made a mistake. The choice of the provider breaks the rule.
No hacker is needed. The law is the problem, not an attack.
cards.answer: A compliance risk
cards.explanation: A law or contract rule is not followed. This is a compliance risk.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Risks Associated with Hardware, Software, and Services”.

cards.question: What is the supply chain in security?
options: Only the trucks that bring new computers to the office each month
Only the servers and laptops that the company owns and runs itself
All the outside suppliers of hardware, software, and services
The list of all the people who work in the company
options_why: Delivery is a small part. Software and services are part of the chain too.
Those are the company's own assets. The supply chain is about outside suppliers.
Workers are inside the company. The supply chain is made of outside suppliers.
cards.answer: All the outside suppliers of hardware, software, and services
cards.explanation: The chain is made of every vendor that the company depends on. Each one is a link.

cards.question: Which item is an example of hardware that a vendor can supply?
options: A program that the vendor sells
A server that the vendor sells
A cloud storage plan that the vendor rents out
A help line that the vendor runs
options_why: A program is software. Hardware is a machine you can touch.
Renting storage is a service, not a machine you buy.
A help line is a service. Hardware is a machine you can touch.
cards.answer: A server that the vendor sells
cards.explanation: Hardware is a machine you can touch. The other items are software or services.

cards.question: What is the supply chain in cybersecurity? Say it in your own words.
cards.answer: All the suppliers (vendors) that a company needs for hardware, software, and services. Each one is a link that can break.
cards.explanation: Think of the bike chain.

cards.question: A company wants to add a program bought from a software vendor. What should the security manager do FIRST?
options: Install the program on every computer to test it
Ask the vendor to give a lower price
Wait until a problem happens, then react
Look at the security risk that this vendor can bring
options_why: This could spread a problem to the whole company before anyone has checked the vendor.
Price is a business question. It does not tell you if the vendor is safe.
Waiting is reactive. A manager should prevent problems, not wait for them.
cards.answer: Look at the security risk that this vendor can bring
cards.explanation: First evaluate the risk. Then choose controls. A manager checks before acting.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: you must evaluate the security risk of your entire supply chain.

cards.question: A company will move its customer data to a cloud provider. Which action is the BEST way to lower the risk?
options: Check that the provider meets the legal and contract rules
Trust the provider because it is a big and well-known company
Buy the most expensive plan of the provider
Let each team choose its own cloud provider
options_why: A big name does not prove good security. You must check.
A high price does not prove that the provider meets your rules.
Without a common check, some providers may break the rules.
cards.answer: Check that the provider meets the legal and contract rules
cards.explanation: The manual warns about providers that do not meet the data rules of a law or a contract. Checking first prevents the problem.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Risks Associated with Hardware, Software, and Services”.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT part of a company's supply chain?
options: The cloud provider that stores its data abroad
The sales team that works inside the company
The vendor that sells its accounting program
The company that repairs its servers
options_why: A cloud provider is an outside supplier of services. It is a link in the chain.
A software vendor is an outside supplier. It is a link in the chain.
A repair company is an outside supplier of services. It is a link in the chain.
cards.answer: The sales team that works inside the company
cards.explanation: The chain is made of outside suppliers. People who work inside the company are not part of it.

cards.question: What does CSP stand for?
cards.answer: Cloud service provider. It is a company that rents out its servers over the internet.
cards.explanation: A CSP is one kind of vendor: it gives you services over the internet.

cards.question: A company checks only its own computers. Which risk is it MOST likely to miss?
options: A short password on one of its own servers
An old laptop in one of its own offices
A weak security practice at one of its suppliers
A broken printer in the company building
options_why: This is inside the company, so a check of its own computers can find it.
This is also inside the company. A check of its own computers can find it.
This is inside the company, and it is not a main security risk.
cards.answer: A weak security practice at one of its suppliers
cards.explanation: Suppliers are outside the company. A check of your own computers cannot see what happens there.

cards.question: A cloud provider does not meet the data rules that your contract needs. What can happen?
options: Nothing, because the cloud provider has its own rules
Your company can face security risks and compliance risks
Only the provider is at risk
Only the price of the service goes up
options_why: Your law and your contract still apply to your company.
The risk reaches your company too, because it is your data.
The manual speaks about security and compliance risks, not about price.
cards.answer: Your company can face security risks and compliance risks
cards.explanation: If the provider does not meet the rules, your company can break the law or the contract. It can also lose data security.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Risks Associated with Hardware, Software, and Services”.

cards.question: A manager learns that a supplier had a data leak. What should the manager do FIRST?
options: End every contract with the supplier today, before any talks
Tell the press about the leak
Find out what data the supplier has and what the risk is
Ask all workers to change their passwords
options_why: This is extreme. It acts before anyone knows the facts.
This is not the first step. Facts come before news.
This is a technical step. It may not even be linked to the leak.
cards.answer: Find out what data the supplier has and what the risk is
cards.explanation: A manager evaluates before acting. First learn the facts, then choose the action.
cards.explanation_more: Outside the manual: this is the usual exam way of thinking (evaluate before you act).

cards.question: Name two risks when you use a cloud provider.
cards.answer: The provider may keep your data in a country where the law does not allow it (compliance risk). It may also not meet the data security rules of your law or contract.
cards.explanation: Both risks are in the manual.

cards.question: What does the word “vendor” mean?
options: A person who works inside the company every day
A law that sets the security rules for a company
A program that watches the network all the time
A company that sells things to other companies
options_why: A worker is inside the company. A vendor is outside.
A law is a rule. A vendor is a company.
A program is software. A vendor is a company.
cards.answer: A company that sells things to other companies
cards.explanation: A vendor is a supplier. Each vendor is a link in the supply chain.

cards.question: Why do you check a supplier before you sign a contract?
cards.answer: Its weak security can become your risk. You must evaluate the risk of the whole chain.
cards.explanation: Think of the yogurt supplier.

concepts.name: Malicious code in the supply chain

paragraphes: Your phone shows an update for an app. You tap Install without thinking. It comes from the maker of the app, so you trust it.
Now imagine that a hacker hid a trap inside that update before it was sent. The trap is a Trojan: a hidden program inside normal software. Everyone who installs the update gets the trap.
The hacker did not attack the victims. The hacker attacked their supplier. This is a supply chain attack.

decouverte.comme: A letter has the stamp of the post office. If someone puts a trap in the envelope before the stamp, everyone thinks the letter is real.
decouverte.enVrai: A software vendor signs its updates. This is called code signing. It is a digital stamp that shows the update comes from the vendor. If the trap is added before the stamp, the stamp is still good. The picture stops here: the stamp shows who sent the update. It does not show that the update is safe.

decouverte.texte: Most companies buy ready-made programs. The name for this is COTS: commercial off-the-shelf software. It is like a boxed game from a shop shelf. You cannot see how it is built. So you must trust the security practices of the vendor. Sometimes the vendor becomes a way to bring in weak spots.

decouverte.question: In 2017, an official update of a known program had a Trojan inside. Why did so many people install it?
options: It came from the vendor that they trusted
It promised free money
It came in an email from a stranger
decouverte.answer: It came from the vendor that they trusted
decouverte.explanation: People trusted the vendor. Here, the trust was the weak spot. Free money and strangers trap people too, but not in this case.

decouverte.texte: The maker of CCleaner, an antivirus product, sent a normal update to its users. A remote-access Trojan was inside. This lets an attacker control a computer from far away. The trap was added before the code was signed. So most users saw a real update. The manual reports more than 2 billion downloads.

In 2020, a company called FireEye shared news of a huge attack. It is called SUNBURST. It used Orion, a SolarWinds product that helps companies watch their IT systems. SUNBURST is a vulnerability: a weak spot that an attacker can use. The tool made to protect became the weapon. Microsoft, Intel, U.S. government agencies, and FireEye itself were victims. SolarWinds thinks about 18,000 companies were hit.

cards.question: Official definition: “COTS”
cards.answer: The widespread use of proprietary commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) software requires customers to trust the security practices of the vendors.
cards.explanation: In simple words: COTS software is bought ready-made. You cannot see how it is built, so you must trust the vendor.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Malicious Code in the Supply Chain”. Off-the-shelf means taken from the store shelf, like a boxed game.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “COTS”?
options: The widespread use of proprietary commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) software requires customers to trust the security practices of the vendors.
The widespread use of proprietary commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) software requires vendors to trust the security practices of the customers.
The widespread use of proprietary commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) software removes the need for customers to trust the security practices of the vendors.
The widespread use of proprietary custom-built software requires customers to trust the security practices of the vendors.
options_why: The roles are swapped. In the real sentence, the customers must trust the vendors.
Buying ready-made software does not remove trust. The real sentence says it requires trust.
COTS means ready-made software from a shelf, not software built just for one customer.
cards.answer: The widespread use of proprietary commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) software requires customers to trust the security practices of the vendors.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: commercial off-the-shelf, customers trust, security practices of the vendors.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “COTS” from memory.
cards.answer: The widespread use of proprietary commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) software requires customers to trust the security practices of the vendors.
cards.explanation: Three ideas: ready-made software, the customer must trust, the vendor's security practices.

cards.question: Official definition: “SUNBURST”
cards.answer: SUNBURST is a vulnerability within the SolarWinds Orion Platform, which, if present and activated, allows an attacker to compromise the server on which the Orion product is running.
cards.explanation: In simple words: SUNBURST is a hidden weak spot in a trusted tool. It lets attackers take over the server.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “SolarWinds and the SUNBURST Attack”. FireEye revealed the attack in 2020.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “SUNBURST”?
options: SUNBURST is a vulnerability within the SolarWinds Orion Platform, which, even if not activated, allows an attacker to compromise the server on which the Orion product is running.
SUNBURST is a vulnerability within the SolarWinds Orion Platform, which, if present and activated, allows an attacker to compromise the server on which the Orion product is running.
SUNBURST is a vulnerability within the SolarWinds Orion Platform, which, if present and activated, allows an attacker to compromise every computer that uses the Orion product.
SUNBURST is a vulnerability within the Microsoft Orion Platform, which, if present and activated, allows an attacker to compromise the server on which the Orion product is running.
options_why: The real sentence has a condition: the weak spot must be present and activated.
The real sentence is about the server where Orion runs, not every computer that uses it.
The Orion Platform belongs to SolarWinds, not to Microsoft.
cards.answer: SUNBURST is a vulnerability within the SolarWinds Orion Platform, which, if present and activated, allows an attacker to compromise the server on which the Orion product is running.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: vulnerability, SolarWinds Orion Platform, present and activated, compromise the server.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “SUNBURST” from memory.
cards.answer: SUNBURST is a vulnerability within the SolarWinds Orion Platform, which, if present and activated, allows an attacker to compromise the server on which the Orion product is running.
cards.explanation: Three ideas: a weak spot in Orion, it must be present and activated, the server is compromised.

cards.question: What is a Trojan?
options: A hidden program inside normal software
A backup copy of the program
A tool that checks software signatures
A law about software vendors
options_why: A backup copy is a safe copy. A Trojan is a trap.
That tool helps the defenders. A Trojan is the trap.
A law is a rule. A Trojan is a program.
cards.answer: A hidden program inside normal software
cards.explanation: The user thinks the software is normal, but a hidden program is inside it.

cards.question: A company installs the official update of its accounting software. The update has a trap inside. What is used against the company?
options: A weak password of one worker
A fake email from a stranger
Its trust in the vendor
A broken firewall at the company
options_why: No password was guessed. The update came from the real vendor.
The update did not come from a stranger. It came from the real vendor.
A firewall is not the issue here. The trap came inside a real update.
cards.answer: Its trust in the vendor
cards.explanation: The company trusts its vendor, so it installs the update. The attacker uses this trust.

cards.question: Which situation is a supply chain attack?
options: A hacker guesses a worker's password and signs in to the system
A worker loses a laptop on a train
A storm floods the building of the company
A hacker hides a Trojan in a vendor's update before it is sent
options_why: The hacker attacked the worker. A supply chain attack goes through a supplier.
This is a loss by accident. No supplier is attacked.
This is a natural event. It is not an attack through a supplier.
cards.answer: A hacker hides a Trojan in a vendor's update before it is sent
cards.explanation: In a supply chain attack, the hacker attacks the supplier. The customers are hit through the supplier.

cards.question: What makes an attack through a software vendor so effective?
cards.answer: Customers trust the updates of the vendor, so they install them. The trap looks like normal software.
cards.explanation: The trust is the weak spot.

cards.question: A company uses ready-made software from a vendor. Which action is the BEST way to lower the risk of a trapped update?
options: Check the vendor's security practices and keep watching
Trust every update because it is signed by the vendor
Stop all updates for ever, even the ones that fix weak spots
Ask workers to avoid the software when they can do so
options_why: A signature shows who sent the update. It does not show that the update is safe.
This is extreme. Updates also fix weak spots.
This is a personal choice, not a control that the company can count on.
cards.answer: Check the vendor's security practices and keep watching
cards.explanation: The manual says customers must trust the vendors. So a company should check how the vendors work, and keep checking.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, sections “Malicious Code in the Supply Chain” and “Third-Party Assessment and Monitoring”.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a reason why attackers like supply chain attacks?
options: Users trust the updates of their vendor
One update can reach many customers
The update always comes from an unknown sender
A signed update looks like a real update
options_why: This is the main reason. The updates come from a trusted source.
This is a reason: one trap can hit many victims. The CCleaner case reached billions of downloads.
This is a reason: the trap can be added before the signature.
cards.answer: The update always comes from an unknown sender
cards.explanation: The attack works because the update comes from a trusted source, not from an unknown sender.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Malicious Code in the Supply Chain”.

cards.question: Why did MOST users think the CCleaner update was real?
options: The update was sent by email to every user
The trap was added before the code was signed
The Trojan was too small to see
The update was free
options_why: The manual says it was a routine update from the vendor, not an email.
The size of the trap is not the reason. The signature made the update look real.
A free price does not make an update look real.
cards.answer: The trap was added before the code was signed
cards.explanation: The signature was valid, because the trap was added first. The whole package looked legitimate.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Malicious Code in the Supply Chain”.

cards.question: Which company shared the news of the SUNBURST attack, and in which year?
cards.answer: FireEye, in 2020.
cards.explanation: FireEye was also one of the victims.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “SolarWinds and the SUNBURST Attack”.

cards.question: Which product was used in the SUNBURST attack?
options: CCleaner
A FireEye scanner
A Microsoft server
SolarWinds Orion
options_why: CCleaner is the 2017 case. SUNBURST came in 2020.
FireEye is the company that revealed the attack. Its product was not the way in.
Microsoft was one of the victims. It was not the product that carried the trap.
cards.answer: SolarWinds Orion
cards.explanation: SUNBURST is a weak spot in the SolarWinds Orion Platform.

cards.question: Security staff learn that the IT monitoring tool of the company has a hidden weak spot. What should the manager do FIRST?
options: Find out how the weak spot can affect its systems
Remove the tool from every system in the company at once
Wait for the vendor to say what to do
Blame the vendor in public
options_why: This is extreme. Monitoring may stop everywhere without a plan.
Waiting is passive. A manager should assess the risk now.
This does not lower the risk. Facts come first.
cards.answer: Find out how the weak spot can affect its systems
cards.explanation: A manager evaluates the risk before acting. Then the company can choose a good control.
cards.explanation_more: Outside the manual: this is the usual exam way of thinking (evaluate before you act).

cards.question: Which attack had more than 2 billion downloads of the bad software, according to the manual?
options: SUNBURST, in 2020
CCleaner, in the year 2020
SUNBURST, in 2017
CCleaner, in 2017
options_why: SUNBURST hit about 18,000 companies. The 2 billion downloads belong to CCleaner.
The CCleaner update was in 2017, not in 2020.
SUNBURST was revealed in 2020.
cards.answer: CCleaner, in 2017
cards.explanation: The manual reports more than 2 billion downloads of the bad CCleaner update in 2017.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Malicious Code in the Supply Chain”.

cards.question: What can a remote-access Trojan do?
cards.answer: It lets an attacker control a computer from far away.
cards.explanation: It was inside the CCleaner update.

cards.question: Why is it so bad that SUNBURST went through a SolarWinds product?
options: The tool was made to sell hardware, not software
A tool that should watch systems became a way to harm them
The tool was used only by small companies
The tool was the first product ever to be attacked by hackers
options_why: Orion is a tool to watch and manage IT systems.
The manual says companies large and small used it.
The manual does not say this. The point is that a protecting tool became the harm.
cards.answer: A tool that should watch systems became a way to harm them
cards.explanation: The manual says that what should keep an eye on IT systems became the tool of harm for those systems.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “SolarWinds and the SUNBURST Attack”.

cards.question: About how many companies did SolarWinds say were affected by SUNBURST?
cards.answer: About 18,000 companies around the world.
cards.explanation: Remember the order of size: thousands, not millions.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “SolarWinds and the SUNBURST Attack”.

paragraphes: The school picks a new caterer for the end-of-year party. The caterer promises perfect meals. The principal believes the promise.
On the day, everyone sees that the kitchen is dirty. A visit before the party would have shown it.
An outside company that does work for you is a third party. You must check it first, and then keep watching it. This is third-party assessment and monitoring.

decouverte.comme: Before hiring the caterer, the principal visits the kitchen and reads its cleaning reports. Later, the principal comes back from time to time.
decouverte.enVrai: A company does the same with its suppliers. It checks their security before it signs. Then it checks again and keeps watching. The picture stops here: you cannot always visit a supplier in another country. That is why the manual says “where feasible”, which means when it is possible.

decouverte.question: The caterer passed the visit in January. Should you check again in June?
options: Yes, you check again regularly
No, one visit is enough
Only after an accident
decouverte.explanation: A supplier changes: new workers, new methods. The manual asks you to re-assess regularly and to monitor all the time. Waiting for an accident is tempting, but then it is too late.

decouverte.titre: Three ways to check a supplier
decouverte.texte: The manual names three checks. An onsite security survey is a visit to look at security on the spot. A formal security audit is a step-by-step review of the systems. Penetration testing is when experts, with permission, try to break in to find weak spots.

The manual says a company needs a third-party risk management policy. The policy is the rule that says what to do. It creates a program: the team and the work that really assess, monitor, and control the risks. This is needed when work is outsourced. Outsourcing means giving a task to an outside company.

A company wants to hire a payroll provider. It compares the provider's practices with its own security requirements. One access control is missing. The company writes down this gap and watches it closely.

cards.question: Official definition: “third-party risk management policy”
cards.answer: Any organization that does business with contractors, vendors, or any other third parties should have a third-party risk management policy that establishes a third-party risk management program responsible for assessing, monitoring, and controlling risks associated with outsourcing to third parties.
cards.explanation: In simple words: a company needs a rule, the policy. The rule creates a program that assesses, monitors, and controls the risks of outside companies.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Third-Party Assessment and Monitoring”.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “third-party risk management policy”?
options: Any organization that does business with contractors, vendors, or any other third parties may have a third-party risk management policy that establishes a third-party risk management program responsible for assessing, monitoring, and controlling risks associated with outsourcing to third parties.

Any organization that does business with contractors, vendors, or any other third parties should have a third-party risk management policy that establishes a third-party risk management program responsible for hiring, paying, and replacing the third parties that cause risks.

Any organization that does business with contractors, vendors, or any other third parties should have a third-party risk management policy that establishes a third-party risk management program responsible for assessing, monitoring, and controlling risks associated with outsourcing to third parties.

Any organization that does business with contractors, vendors, or any other third parties should have a third-party risk management policy that establishes a third-party risk management program responsible only for assessing risks associated with outsourcing to third parties.
options_why: The real sentence says should, not may. The policy is not a choice.
The program is about assessing, monitoring, and controlling risks, not about hiring or paying.
The program does three things: assess, monitor, and control. Not only assess.
cards.answer: Any organization that does business with contractors, vendors, or any other third parties should have a third-party risk management policy that establishes a third-party risk management program responsible for assessing, monitoring, and controlling risks associated with outsourcing to third parties.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: should have, policy, program, assessing, monitoring, and controlling.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “third-party risk management policy” from memory.
cards.answer: Any organization that does business with contractors, vendors, or any other third parties should have a third-party risk management policy that establishes a third-party risk management program responsible for assessing, monitoring, and controlling risks associated with outsourcing to third parties.
cards.explanation: Remember three verbs: assess, monitor, control. The policy decides, and the program acts.

cards.question: Official definition: “oversight of third parties”
cards.answer: Governance and oversight activities should include onsite security surveys, formal security audits of third-party systems, and penetration testing, where feasible.
cards.explanation: In simple words: check suppliers with a visit, an audit, and a test. Do it when it is possible.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Third-Party Assessment and Monitoring”. The manual points to chapter 6 for audits.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “oversight of third parties”?
options: Governance and oversight activities should include onsite security surveys, formal security audits of third-party systems, and penetration testing, in every case.
Governance and oversight activities should include onsite security surveys, formal security audits of third-party systems, and penetration testing, where feasible.
Governance and oversight activities should include onsite security surveys, formal security audits of third-party systems, and employee background checks, where feasible.
Governance and oversight activities should include only onsite security surveys and formal security audits of third-party systems, where feasible.
options_why: The real sentence says where feasible. Some checks are not always possible.
The third activity is penetration testing, not background checks.
The real sentence has three activities. Penetration testing is one of them.
cards.answer: Governance and oversight activities should include onsite security surveys, formal security audits of third-party systems, and penetration testing, where feasible.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: onsite security surveys, formal security audits, penetration testing, where feasible.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “oversight of third parties” from memory.
cards.answer: Governance and oversight activities should include onsite security surveys, formal security audits of third-party systems, and penetration testing, where feasible.
cards.explanation: Three checks: visit, audit, test. And always where feasible.

cards.question: Official definition: “assessing a new third party”
cards.answer: Any new third party should be assessed against your organization's security requirements, and gaps should be documented and closely monitored.
cards.explanation: In simple words: check a new supplier against your rules. Write down the gaps and watch them closely.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Third-Party Assessment and Monitoring”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “assessing a new third party” from memory.
cards.answer: Any new third party should be assessed against your organization's security requirements, and gaps should be documented and closely monitored.
cards.explanation: Three ideas: assess against your requirements, document the gaps, and monitor them closely.

cards.question: What is a third party?
options: A person who works in your own security team
A rule that sets the lowest level of security
A manager who reviews the work of a team
An outside company that works for you
options_why: A person on your team is inside the company. A third party is outside.
That is a different idea. A third party is a company, not a rule.
A manager works inside the company. A third party is outside.
cards.answer: An outside company that works for you
cards.explanation: A third party is not part of your company. Contractors and vendors are third parties.

cards.question: Which activity is a penetration test?
options: Experts try to break in, with permission
A visit to the supplier to look at its security
A step-by-step review of the systems of the supplier
A contract that lists the promises of the supplier
options_why: That is an onsite security survey.
That is a formal security audit.
That is a different document. It is not a test of the systems.
cards.answer: Experts try to break in, with permission
cards.explanation: A penetration test is a safe attack, done with permission, to find weak spots.

cards.question: What does a third-party risk management policy create?
options: A list of the cheapest suppliers
A team that writes new software and programs for outside companies
A program that assesses, monitors, and controls third-party risks
A contract that fixes the price of a service
options_why: A policy is about risk, not about price.
The program watches suppliers. It does not write software for them.
A contract sets the price. A policy sets how to manage risk.
cards.answer: A program that assesses, monitors, and controls third-party risks
cards.explanation: The policy is the rule. The program is the team and the work that follow the rule.

cards.question: What is an onsite security survey?
cards.answer: A visit to a supplier to look at its security on the spot.
cards.explanation: One of the three oversight activities in the manual.

cards.question: Which word in the policy sentence means giving a task to an outside company?
options: Auditing
Continuous monitoring
Assessing
Outsourcing
options_why: Auditing means reviewing. It does not mean giving a task away.
Monitoring means watching. It does not mean giving a task away.
Assessing means judging the risk. It does not mean giving a task away.
cards.answer: Outsourcing
cards.explanation: Outsourcing means giving a task to an outside company.

cards.question: A new supplier lacks two controls that your company requires. What should the manager do FIRST?
options: Sign the contract and forget the gaps
Cancel the plan without any talk
Write down the gaps and watch them closely
Add the missing controls to your own systems
options_why: The gaps are a risk for your company. They must not be forgotten.
This is extreme. The manual says to document the gaps and monitor them.
The gap is at the supplier. Your own systems do not fix it.
cards.answer: Write down the gaps and watch them closely
cards.explanation: The manual says that gaps should be documented and closely monitored.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Third-Party Assessment and Monitoring”.

cards.question: Which action is the BEST way to keep a supplier safe over time?
options: Assess the supplier once, before it signs
Re-assess the supplier regularly and monitor it all the time
Assess the supplier only after an incident
Trust the supplier because its contract is long
options_why: A supplier changes. One check is not enough.
This is reactive. The manual asks for regular checks and monitoring.
A long contract does not prove good security.
cards.answer: Re-assess the supplier regularly and monitor it all the time
cards.explanation: The manual says that third parties should be re-assessed regularly and continuously monitored.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Third-Party Assessment and Monitoring”.

cards.question: What is a formal security audit?
cards.answer: A step-by-step review of the systems of a third party.
cards.explanation: One of the three oversight activities in the manual.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT an oversight activity named in the manual?
options: Waiting for the supplier to send a letter each year
An onsite security survey
A formal security audit of the supplier's systems
Penetration testing, where feasible
options_why: The manual names this activity: a visit to look at security on the spot.
The manual names this activity: a step-by-step review.
The manual names this activity: a test, with permission.
cards.answer: Waiting for the supplier to send a letter each year
cards.explanation: The three activities are the survey, the audit, and the test. Waiting for a letter is not a real check.

cards.question: According to the manual, what is the MOST difficult part of managing third-party risk?
options: Finding controls that fit the risks
Making sure that third parties really do what they should
Writing the third-party risk management policy
Paying for the audits of the suppliers
options_why: The manual says that, in most cases, the controls are already known.
Writing the policy is not described as the toughest part.
The manual does not talk about the cost of audits.
cards.answer: Making sure that third parties really do what they should
cards.explanation: The controls are often known. The hard part is to make sure that the third parties apply them.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Third-Party Assessment and Monitoring”.

cards.question: A company cannot visit a supplier in another country. Which option is the BEST?
options: Skip all the checks because a visit is not possible
Accept the supplier after it promises to be secure
Use the other possible checks and keep monitoring
Use only suppliers from the same city for ever
options_why: The manual says where feasible. It does not say to skip every check.
A promise is not a check. The company needs proof.
This is extreme. The company can still use other checks.
cards.answer: Use the other possible checks and keep monitoring
cards.explanation: The manual says the checks are needed where feasible. When one check is not possible, use the others.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Third-Party Assessment and Monitoring”.

cards.question: Why does the manual say “where feasible” for these checks?
cards.answer: Sometimes a check is not possible, for example a visit to a supplier far away.
cards.explanation: Use the checks that are possible.

cards.question: A company will give its payroll to an outside provider. What should it do FIRST?
options: Send the payroll data first and check the provider later
Let the provider choose its own security rules
Choose the provider with the lowest price
Compare the provider's practices with its requirements
options_why: The data is at risk before the provider has been checked.
The company's requirements must come first. The provider does not decide them.
Price does not show if the provider is safe.
cards.answer: Compare the provider's practices with its requirements
cards.explanation: A new third party is assessed against your organization's security requirements, before it gets the work.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Third-Party Assessment and Monitoring”.

cards.question: What should a company do with the gaps it finds at a new third party?
cards.answer: Write them down and watch them closely.
cards.explanation: A gap is a place where the supplier does not meet your requirements.

paragraphes: The school picks its meal suppliers. It sets one starting rule for all of them: keep the meat cold and clean the kitchen.
A supplier can do more. If it does less, the school says no.
For a company, this starting rule is called a minimum security requirement (MSR).

decouverte.comme: At a fun park, a sign says: you must be at least this tall. Taller people can ride too. Shorter people cannot.
decouverte.enVrai: An MSR is like that sign. It is the lowest level of security that a company accepts from a supplier. A supplier can be better, but never lower. The picture stops here: the sign does not say how high to aim. It only shows the lowest level.

decouverte.question: A law sets a security rule. Your company wants an MSR weaker than the law. Is it allowed?
options: No: an MSR cannot be below the law
Yes: the company makes its own rules
Yes, if the supplier is small
decouverte.answer: No: an MSR cannot be below the law
decouverte.explanation: The manual says not to set an MSR below an outside requirement, such as a law or a contract. The company is the boss at home, but the law comes first.

decouverte.texte: A clinic must follow a law that protects health data. It writes MSRs for its suppliers. For example: encrypt the data (lock it with a secret code) and keep records of who opens it. The clinic cannot make the MSRs weaker than the law. It must also check, with an audit, that each supplier follows them.

Security posture means the overall state of a company's security. Think of how healthy a person is. A company hopes for the strongest posture from its suppliers. The MSR only fixes the lowest level it accepts.

cards.question: Official definition: “minimum security requirements (MSRs)”
cards.answer: Similar to baselines and standards (discussed earlier in this chapter), your organization should establish minimum security requirements (MSRs) that define the least acceptable security standards that vendors and other parties in your supply chain must satisfy.
cards.explanation: In simple words: the MSRs are the lowest level of security that a supplier must reach. Baselines and standards are the security rules that a company sets for its own systems.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Minimum Security Requirements”.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “minimum security requirements (MSRs)”?
options: Similar to baselines and standards (discussed earlier in this chapter), your organization should establish minimum security requirements (MSRs) that define the least acceptable security standards that vendors and other parties in your supply chain must satisfy.

Similar to baselines and standards (discussed earlier in this chapter), your organization should establish minimum security requirements (MSRs) that define the best possible security standards that vendors and other parties in your supply chain must satisfy.

Similar to baselines and standards (discussed earlier in this chapter), your organization should establish minimum security requirements (MSRs) that define the least acceptable security standards that your own employees and departments must satisfy.

Similar to baselines and standards (discussed earlier in this chapter), your organization should establish minimum security requirements (MSRs) that define the average security standards that vendors and other parties in your supply chain must satisfy.
options_why: An MSR is the lowest level, not the best possible level.
MSRs are for vendors and other parties in the supply chain, not for your own workers.
The real sentence says least acceptable, not average.
cards.answer: Similar to baselines and standards (discussed earlier in this chapter), your organization should establish minimum security requirements (MSRs) that define the least acceptable security standards that vendors and other parties in your supply chain must satisfy.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: minimum, least acceptable, vendors and other parties in your supply chain.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “minimum security requirements (MSRs)” from memory.
cards.answer: Similar to baselines and standards (discussed earlier in this chapter), your organization should establish minimum security requirements (MSRs) that define the least acceptable security standards that vendors and other parties in your supply chain must satisfy.
cards.explanation: Three ideas: set the MSRs, the lowest level you accept, and who must meet them.

cards.question: Official definition: “what an MSR describes”
cards.answer: Of course, you should strive to ensure that your third parties have the strongest possible security postures, but MSRs, as the name suggests, describe the lowest level of security that your organization is willing to accept from a third party.
cards.explanation: In simple words: you hope for the strongest security, but the MSR only says the lowest level that you accept.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Minimum Security Requirements”. A security posture is the overall state of security.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “what an MSR describes” from memory.
cards.answer: Of course, you should strive to ensure that your third parties have the strongest possible security postures, but MSRs, as the name suggests, describe the lowest level of security that your organization is willing to accept from a third party.
cards.explanation: Three ideas: aim for the strongest, the MSR is the lowest level, and the organization accepts it.

cards.question: What does an MSR describe?
options: The highest level of security that a supplier can reach
The price that the company pays for security
The lowest level of security the company accepts
The number of suppliers that the company can use
options_why: That is the opposite. An MSR is a floor, not a top.
An MSR is about the level of security, not about money.
An MSR sets a level of security, not a number of suppliers.
cards.answer: The lowest level of security the company accepts
cards.explanation: An MSR is the floor. A supplier must reach it, and it can go higher.

cards.question: A supplier is much better than the MSR. What does this mean?
options: It breaks the MSR, because it does more than asked
It is accepted, because it is above the lowest level
It must lower its security to match the MSR
It is accepted only if it is cheap
options_why: Doing more is fine. The MSR only sets the lowest level.
A company hopes for the strongest security. There is no reason to lower it.
The MSR is about security, not price.
cards.answer: It is accepted, because it is above the lowest level
cards.explanation: The MSR is a floor. A supplier above the floor is accepted.

cards.question: An MSR says: encrypt the data and keep records of who opens it. Which supplier meets it?
options: One that encrypts data and keeps access records
One that encrypts data but keeps no records
One that keeps records but does not encrypt data
One that promises to do both next year
options_why: One part of the MSR is missing. The supplier must do both.
One part of the MSR is missing. The supplier must do both.
A promise for later does not meet the MSR today.
cards.answer: One that encrypts data and keeps access records
cards.explanation: A supplier must meet every part of the MSR, today.

cards.question: What does MSR stand for?
cards.answer: Minimum security requirements.
cards.explanation: The lowest level of security that a company accepts from a supplier.

cards.question: What does security posture mean?
options: A list of all the passwords of a company
The number of firewalls in a building
The yearly cost of the security team
The overall state of an organization's security
options_why: A list of passwords is data. Posture is the overall state.
A number of tools is only one detail. Posture is the whole picture.
Cost is only one detail. Posture is the overall state.
cards.answer: The overall state of an organization's security
cards.explanation: Posture is the whole picture of how strong the security is.

cards.question: A law says that suppliers must encrypt health data. How should the company write its MSR about this?
options: Weaker than the law, to keep more suppliers
Without any link to the law
At least as strict as the law
The same as the rules of the cheapest supplier
options_why: The manual says an MSR must not be below an outside requirement.
The law is an outside requirement that the MSR must respect.
Price does not set the level of security. The law does.
cards.answer: At least as strict as the law
cards.explanation: The manual says not to set an MSR below any external compliance requirement.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Minimum Security Requirements”.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT something an MSR should take into account?
options: The wish of a supplier to use weaker rules
Legal requirements
Contract requirements
Regulatory requirements
options_why: The manual says an MSR should take legal requirements into account.
The manual says an MSR should take contract requirements into account.
The manual says an MSR should take regulatory requirements into account.
cards.answer: The wish of a supplier to use weaker rules
cards.explanation: An MSR follows the law, the contracts, and the regulations. A supplier cannot lower it.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Minimum Security Requirements”.

cards.question: What must a company do after it sets and shares its MSRs?
cards.answer: Be ready to audit and assess if the third parties follow them.
cards.explanation: Writing the MSRs is not enough.

cards.question: A company has set and shared its MSRs. Which task comes AFTER that?
options: Remove the MSRs, because the suppliers know them
Audit and assess if the third parties follow the MSRs
Wait for the suppliers to report their own problems
Raise the MSRs every month
options_why: The MSRs must stay. They are the base of the checks.
Waiting is reactive. The company should check.
The manual does not say this. The next step is to check compliance.
cards.answer: Audit and assess if the third parties follow the MSRs
cards.explanation: The manual says you must be ready to audit and assess third parties against the MSRs.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Minimum Security Requirements”.

cards.question: A supplier says: our security is below your MSR, but our price is good. What is the BEST answer?
options: Accept it, because the price is good
Accept it for one year, then check again later
Lower the MSR for this supplier only
It is not accepted until it meets the MSR
options_why: Price does not replace the MSR. The MSR is the lowest level you accept.
The company would accept a risk below its own lowest level.
Lowering the MSR breaks the idea of a common minimum.
cards.answer: It is not accepted until it meets the MSR
cards.explanation: An MSR is the lowest level the company accepts. A supplier below it does not qualify.
cards.explanation_more: Outside the manual: this is the usual exam way of thinking (policy before price).

cards.question: Which statement about an MSR is MOST correct?
options: It is a floor: suppliers should aim higher
It is a target: suppliers should aim for exactly this level
It is a limit: suppliers must not go above it
It is a price: suppliers pay it to join the chain
options_why: The manual says to aim for the strongest security, not only for the minimum.
Suppliers can always do better. The MSR is the lowest level.
An MSR is about security, not money.
cards.answer: It is a floor: suppliers should aim higher
cards.explanation: The MSR is the lowest level accepted. The company still hopes for the strongest posture.

cards.question: Should a company aim only for the minimum from its suppliers? Say why.
cards.answer: No. It should aim for the strongest security. The MSR only sets the lowest level that it accepts.
cards.explanation: Think of the height sign.

cards.question: A company writes MSRs for its suppliers. What should it check FIRST, so the MSRs are not too weak?
options: The MSRs that a competitor uses for its suppliers
The rules of the cheapest supplier we can find
The wishes of the sales team
The legal, contract, and regulatory rules
options_why: Another company has other rules. Your own rules come first.
The cheapest supplier is not the base for your security.
The sales team does not set the security level.
cards.answer: The legal, contract, and regulatory rules
cards.explanation: An MSR must not be below any outside requirement, so you first learn what these requirements are.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Minimum Security Requirements”.

cards.question: Why must an MSR not be lower than a law?
cards.answer: The law is an outside requirement that the company must follow. The MSR cannot go under it.
cards.explanation: Think of the clinic and the health data law.

paragraphes: Your school signs a contract with the cafeteria. It says: lunch is ready before half past twelve, every day.
A month later, lunch comes at two o'clock. The school shows the contract and asks for a fix.
In computing, this kind of contract is called a service-level agreement (SLA).

decouverte.comme: A pizza shop says: in 30 minutes, or it is free. If the pizza is late, you have rights.
decouverte.enVrai: An SLA works the same way. The provider promises a minimum level of performance, in a contract. If it breaks the promise, the customer has rights. The picture stops here: an SLA is a signed, exact contract. It is more than a promise in words.

decouverte.question: Your cloud provider is down for a long time. Your SLA promises that the system works almost all the time. What can the SLA give you?
options: Money back, or a way to leave without a penalty
Nothing, because a breakdown is normal
Only an apology
decouverte.answer: Money back, or a way to leave without a penalty
decouverte.explanation: The SLA is a contract, so the provider must keep its promise. If it does not, the customer can get money, or end the service with no penalty.

decouverte.texte: A company rents servers from a cloud provider. The SLA promises a level of uptime. Uptime is the time when the service works. After a long outage, when the service is down, the company may get money back. It may also end the service with no penalty.

An MSR says the lowest level of security that a supplier must reach. An SLA says the lowest level of performance that a provider promises. Both help a company to hold a third party accountable. Accountable means that the third party must answer for its work.

cards.question: Official definition: “service-level agreement (SLA)”
cards.answer: A service-level agreement (SLA) is a contractual agreement between a service provider and its customers that establishes the minimum performance standards that the provider is obligated to meet.
cards.explanation: In simple words: an SLA is a contract. The provider must reach a minimum level of performance. It has no choice.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Service-Level Requirements”.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “service-level agreement (SLA)”?
options: A service-level agreement (SLA) is a contractual agreement between a service provider and its customers that establishes the maximum performance standards that the provider is obligated to meet.
A service-level agreement (SLA) is a contractual agreement between a service provider and its customers that establishes the minimum performance standards that the provider is obligated to meet.
A service-level agreement (SLA) is a contractual agreement between a service provider and its customers that establishes the minimum performance standards that the provider is encouraged to meet.
A service-level agreement (SLA) is a contractual agreement between a service provider and its customers that establishes the minimum cost standards that the provider is obligated to meet.
options_why: An SLA sets the minimum level, not the maximum.
The provider is obligated. It has a duty, not just a hope.
An SLA is about performance, not about cost.
cards.answer: A service-level agreement (SLA) is a contractual agreement between a service provider and its customers that establishes the minimum performance standards that the provider is obligated to meet.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: contractual agreement, service provider and customers, minimum performance standards, obligated.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “service-level agreement (SLA)” from memory.
cards.answer: A service-level agreement (SLA) is a contractual agreement between a service provider and its customers that establishes the minimum performance standards that the provider is obligated to meet.
cards.explanation: Four ideas: a contract, a provider and its customers, a minimum level of performance, and a duty.

cards.question: Official definition: “SLAs and third parties”
cards.answer: When dealing with vendors and other third parties, SLAs serve as documented and agreed-upon performance requirements that a customer can use to hold the third party accountable.
cards.explanation: In simple words: the SLA is the written proof that lets you ask a supplier to answer for its work.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Service-Level Requirements”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “SLAs and third parties” from memory.
cards.answer: When dealing with vendors and other third parties, SLAs serve as documented and agreed-upon performance requirements that a customer can use to hold the third party accountable.
cards.explanation: Three ideas: documented and agreed, performance requirements, and holding the third party accountable.

cards.question: What is an SLA?
options: A list of security rules for the company's own workers
A test that tries to break into a provider's systems
A contract in which a provider promises a minimum level of service
A plan to restart work after a disaster
options_why: That is an internal policy. An SLA is a contract with a provider.
That is a penetration test. An SLA is a contract.
That is a different kind of plan. An SLA is a contract with a provider.
cards.answer: A contract in which a provider promises a minimum level of service
cards.explanation: An SLA is a written, agreed promise of performance between a provider and its customer.

cards.question: Your cloud provider was down for several days. The SLA promised high uptime. What can the company get?
options: Nothing, because outages are normal
A free security audit of the provider
The source code of all the programs of the provider
Money back, or the right to leave with no penalty
options_why: The SLA is a contract. A long outage can break it.
The manual does not say this. It speaks about money or ending the service.
An SLA does not give the provider's source code.
cards.answer: Money back, or the right to leave with no penalty
cards.explanation: The manual says that after a long outage, a company may get money back. It may also end the service with no penalty.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Service-Level Requirements”.

cards.question: Who signs an SLA?
options: Two customers of the same provider
A customer and a government office
A service provider and its customer
A provider and its own workers
options_why: Customers do not make a contract between themselves. The provider is a party.
An SLA is between a provider and a customer, not an office.
That would be a work contract. An SLA is made with customers.
cards.answer: A service provider and its customer
cards.explanation: An SLA is an agreement between a service provider and its customers.

cards.question: What does SLA stand for?
cards.answer: Service-level agreement.
cards.explanation: A contract between a service provider and its customers.

cards.question: Which word in the SLA sentence shows that the provider has no choice?
options: Contractual
Obligated
Minimum
Customers
options_why: Contractual says it is a contract. It does not say the provider has a duty.
Minimum says the level is the lowest. It does not say the provider has a duty.
Customers says who gets the service. It does not say the provider has a duty.
cards.answer: Obligated
cards.explanation: Obligated means the provider has a duty to meet the standards.

cards.question: The website of a company, on a cloud provider, is down for several days. What should the manager check FIRST?
options: What the SLA says the provider must do when it fails
Which worker to blame
How to build a new website
How to move to another provider today
options_why: Blame does not fix anything. The contract says what the provider owes.
This is a big step. First learn what the contract says.
This is too fast. First learn the rights in the contract.
cards.answer: What the SLA says the provider must do when it fails
cards.explanation: The SLA is the written promise. A manager reads it before acting.
cards.explanation_more: Outside the manual: this is the usual exam way of thinking (check the contract first).

cards.question: A company chooses a cloud provider. Which promise would be BEST to see in the SLA?
options: A promise that the provider will try its very best
A clear level of uptime, and what happens if missed
A promise that no outage can ever happen
A promise that is only said to the customer by phone
options_why: This is vague. It cannot be measured.
This is extreme. No provider can promise it.
A promise that is not written is hard to prove.
cards.answer: A clear level of uptime, and what happens if missed
cards.explanation: A good SLA has a number that can be measured, and a result if the provider misses it.

cards.question: What can a company get if a provider's service is down for a long time?
cards.answer: Money back (financial compensation), or the right to end the service with no penalty.
cards.explanation: This is an example from the manual.

cards.question: Why is an SLA MOST useful to the customer?
options: It makes the service of the provider cheaper
It lets the customer read the provider's source code
It removes all risk from the provider
It lets the customer hold the provider accountable
options_why: An SLA is about performance, not about price.
An SLA does not give access to source code.
No document removes all risk. An SLA only sets a promise.
cards.answer: It lets the customer hold the provider accountable
cards.explanation: The manual says an SLA is a documented and agreed requirement that a customer can use to hold the third party accountable.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Service-Level Requirements”.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT true about an SLA?
options: It is a contract
It sets a minimum level of performance for the provider
It is only a promise that is said, not written
It says what the provider must meet
options_why: This is true. The word contractual is in the definition.
This is true. It sets the lowest level that the provider must meet.
This is true. The provider is obligated to meet the standards.
cards.answer: It is only a promise that is said, not written
cards.explanation: An SLA is documented and agreed. It is not just a spoken promise.

cards.question: A company writes the lowest level of performance that its cloud provider must give. Which document is this?
options: An SLA
An MSR
A third-party risk management policy
An audit report
options_why: An MSR is the lowest level of security, not of performance.
A policy says how to manage risk. It does not set a performance level.
An audit report shows the result of a review. It does not set a promise.
cards.answer: An SLA
cards.explanation: An SLA sets the minimum performance. An MSR sets the minimum security.

cards.question: What is uptime?
cards.answer: The time when the service works.
cards.explanation: Think of the pizza promise: a number that can be measured.

cards.question: A company has no SLA with its cloud provider. What is the BEST description of the problem?
options: The provider cannot run its servers
It has no written promise to use
The company must stop using the cloud
The provider will always give bad service
options_why: An SLA is not needed to run servers.
The company can still use the cloud. It just has less protection.
The provider may give good service. The company simply cannot hold it accountable.
cards.answer: It has no written promise to use
cards.explanation: Without an SLA, the customer has no documented promise to hold the provider accountable.

cards.question: In your own words: why is an SLA good for the customer?
cards.answer: It is a written, agreed promise. The customer can use it to hold the provider accountable.
cards.explanation: Think of the cafeteria contract.

concepts.name: NIST IR 7622: ten practices for the supply chain

paragraphes: After many stomach bugs in cafeterias, an agency writes ten good habits for kitchens.
A big school kitchen and a small snack bar do not follow them in the same way. Each one fits the habits to its job.
There is a list like this for the supply chain of computer systems. It is called NIST IR 7622. NIST is a U.S. government agency that writes security guides.

decouverte.comme: Sleeping well, moving, and washing your hands are habits that protect your health. A child and an adult do not follow them in the same way.
decouverte.enVrai: NIST IR 7622 is a guide with ten practices to lower supply chain risk. The text says the actions change with each one's role. So do the level and the type of control. The picture stops here: these are exact security practices, not general advice.

decouverte.question: In a chain, you are a small supplier. Your neighbor is a very big maker. Are your controls the same?
options: No: they depend on each one's role
Yes: everyone uses the same ones
Only the big maker needs any
decouverte.answer: No: they depend on each one's role
decouverte.explanation: The manual says the actions, the level, and the type of control change with the role. Everyone takes part, but not in the same way.

decouverte.texte: Some words in the list are hard. Provenance means where something comes from, and who handled it. Defensive design means building a system so that it can resist attacks. Disposal means getting rid of old equipment in a safe way.

First practice: uniquely identify supply chain elements, processes, and actors. This means: keep an exact list of what and who is in the chain. Last practice: manage disposal and final disposition throughout the lifecycle. This means: even the end of life of old equipment is part of security.

CNSS stands for Committee on National Security Systems. Its Directive 505 sets security needs for strategic national systems, which are very important to the country. CNCI number 11 is an initiative. It gives agencies tools to manage their cyber supply chain with a risk-driven approach.

Stop all suppliers from working with the company

cards.answer: Building systems, parts, and processes so that they can resist attacks.

Use defensive design for systems

Defensive design is about how a system is built.
cards.answer: Manage disposal and final disposition throughout the lifecycle

options_why: This is practice number eight in the manual.

Perform supply chain risk management awareness and training

cards.answer: Manage disposal and final disposition activities throughout the system or element lifecycle.

It is a guide only for cloud providers

concepts.name: ISO 28000: a framework for the supply chain

paragraphes: You want better grades in math. You make a study plan. You follow it for a month. Then you check your test results.
You see what worked, and you fix your plan. Then you start again. Slowly, your grades go up, without changing everything at once.
Security standards use the same idea. It is called the PDCA cycle. A standard is a text of good practice. ISO is an international group that publishes standards.

decouverte.comme: Plan your study. Do it. Check your test score. Act: fix what did not work. Then start again.
decouverte.enVrai: PDCA means Plan, Do, Check, Act. Plan: decide what to do. Do: do it. Check: look at the result. Act: fix what needs fixing. A company repeats the cycle to improve its security. The picture stops here: a school year ends, but the PDCA cycle never stops.

decouverte.question: ISO 28000 is about the supply chain. Is it only for cybersecurity?
options: No: it is not specific to cybersecurity
Yes: it talks only about computer security
decouverte.answer: No: it is not specific to cybersecurity
decouverte.explanation: The manual says ISO 28000 is not specific to cybersecurity. It looks at the supply chain in general. Many people think only of computers, which is natural.

decouverte.titre: A standard that adds to the others
decouverte.texte: A company already follows ISO 9001 and ISO 27001. These are two other ISO standards. It adds ISO 28000 for its supply chain. All of it fits into the company's audits and its risk management.

A framework is a ready-made structure to organize your work. A security management system is the set of rules, people, and tasks that run security. Conformance means that the company really follows the security practice.

concepts.name: The 12 principles of the U.K. NCSC

paragraphes: The principal wants to choose good suppliers. She cuts the work into four stages: know who delivers what, set rules, check, then improve.
A country did the same for its companies. It wrote twelve principles and put them into four stages.
These twelve principles come from the national cyber security center of the United Kingdom: the NCSC.

decouverte.comme: To climb stairs, you go from one step to the next. If you skip the first step, you may fall.
decouverte.enVrai: The four NCSC stages go in order: understand the risks, establish control, check your arrangements, and keep improving. Each stage helps the next one. The picture stops here: after the last step, you do not stop. You keep improving.

decouverte.question: You are in charge of the suppliers of your company. Which stage do you start with?
options: Understand the risks: who are my suppliers?
Check my arrangements with them
Look for continuous improvement
decouverte.answer: Understand the risks: who are my suppliers?
decouverte.explanation: You cannot control or check what you do not know. First, you list the suppliers and what needs protection. The other stages come after.

decouverte.texte: Stage 1: the company lists its suppliers and what it must protect. Stage 2: it sets its minimum requirements and shares them. Stage 3: it plans checks that give proof, such as audit rights and KPIs. A KPI is a number that shows if the work goes well. Stage 4: it builds trust and pushes for progress.

cards.explanation: In simple words: the NCSC wrote guidance to help companies know the risks better. It gives 12 principles to keep control of the supply chain.
