options_why: The manual names four stages, not three.
The manual names four stages, not five.
Twelve is the number of principles, not the number of stages.
cards.answer: Four
cards.explanation: The 12 principles are grouped in four stages.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.K. National Cyber Security Centre”.

cards.question: A company lists its vendors and decides what must be protected. Which NCSC stage is it in?
options: Establish control
Check your arrangements
Understand the risks
Continuous improvement
options_why: Control comes after. First the company must know its vendors.
Checking comes third. Here the company is only listing.
Improvement is the last stage.
cards.answer: Understand the risks
cards.explanation: Stage 1 is about identifying the vendors and what needs to be protected.

cards.question: A company writes its minimum security requirements and sends them to its suppliers. Which NCSC stage is it in?
options: Understand the risks
Establish control
Check your arrangements
Continuous improvement
options_why: That stage is about listing the vendors and what to protect.
That stage is about checks that give proof.
That stage is about building trust and progress.
cards.answer: Establish control
cards.explanation: Stage 2 sets the MSRs and tells the suppliers what the company expects.

cards.question: How many principles does the NCSC propose, and in how many stages?
cards.answer: Twelve principles, in four stages.
cards.explanation: Do not mix it up with the ten practices of NIST IR 7622.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.K. National Cyber Security Centre”.

cards.question: What is the aim of the NCSC guidance?
options: To replace ISO 28000
To give a list of approved vendors for every company
To give better awareness and control of supply chain risk
To fine all companies that have weak suppliers in their chain
options_why: The NCSC guidance is another text. It does not replace ISO 28000.
The guidance gives principles, not a list of vendors.
The manual does not speak about fines.
cards.answer: To give better awareness and control of supply chain risk
cards.explanation: The NCSC gives guidance for improved awareness and 12 principles for effective control.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.K. National Cyber Security Centre”.

cards.question: Which NCSC stage should a company do FIRST?
options: Understand the risks, since you cannot control the unknown
Establish control, because rules protect everyone at once
Check your arrangements, because proof is the most important
Continuous improvement, because it saves time
options_why: Rules come second. First you need to know your suppliers.
You need rules before you can check them.
Improvement is the last stage. It needs the first three.
cards.answer: Understand the risks, since you cannot control the unknown
cards.explanation: The stages go in order. Stage 1 lists the vendors and what must be protected.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.K. National Cyber Security Centre”.

cards.question: A company plans audit rights and key performance indicators for its suppliers. Which stage is this?
options: Understand the risks
Check your arrangements
Establish control
Continuous improvement
options_why: Stage 1 is about listing vendors and what must be protected.
Stage 2 is about the minimum requirements and telling suppliers.
Stage 4 is about trust and better security.
cards.answer: Check your arrangements
cards.explanation: Assurance activities, such as audit rights and KPIs, belong to stage 3.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.K. National Cyber Security Centre”.

cards.question: What is an assurance activity?
cards.answer: A check that gives proof that suppliers follow the rules. The manual names audit rights and KPIs.
cards.explanation: Think of a school test.

cards.question: A company has set its MSRs and checked its suppliers. Which action is the BEST next move in the NCSC approach?
options: Stop work, because the four stages are done
End the contracts of all suppliers that are not perfect
Wait for the next audit and do nothing
Keep building trust and push for security improvements
options_why: The last stage is continuous. The work never stops.
This is extreme. The stage asks to encourage progress.
This is passive. The stage asks for constant effort.
cards.answer: Keep building trust and push for security improvements
cards.explanation: Stage 4 is continuous improvement: build trust and encourage better security.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.K. National Cyber Security Centre”.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT an NCSC stage?
options: Understand the risks
Replace the suppliers
Establish control
Check your arrangements
options_why: This is stage 1 in the manual.
This is stage 2 in the manual.
This is stage 3 in the manual.
cards.answer: Replace the suppliers
cards.explanation: The four stages are understand, establish control, check, and improve. Replacing suppliers is not one of them.

cards.question: What is the MOST important result of the “Understand the risks” stage?
options: A list of the vendors and of what must be protected
A signed contract with each vendor
A set of audit reports
A plan to replace all the vendors
options_why: Contracts and requirements come in the next stages.
Audits belong to the check stage.
The stage is about knowing the vendors, not replacing them.
cards.answer: A list of the vendors and of what must be protected
cards.explanation: The stage involves identifying your vendors and what needs to be protected, and why.

cards.question: Why does the “Understand the risks” stage come first?
cards.answer: You cannot control or check what you do not know. First list the vendors and what needs protection.
cards.explanation: Think of the staircase.

cards.question: A company skips the “Check your arrangements” stage. What is the BEST description of the problem?
options: It no longer knows who its suppliers are
It can no longer write MSRs
It cannot know if its suppliers follow the rules
It must start the whole cycle again
options_why: That is stage 1. Here the company only skipped the checks.
MSRs belong to stage 2. The company can still write them.
Nothing forces a restart. The problem is the missing proof.
cards.answer: It cannot know if its suppliers follow the rules
cards.explanation: The checks give proof that the rules are followed. Without them, the company is blind.

cards.question: What does KPI stand for?
cards.answer: Key performance indicator: a number that shows if the work goes well.
cards.explanation: It is one of the checks in stage 3.
